description.purpose: The broker's whole state, as six tables: `policy` (the rules, as ROWS -- politics is changed with an insert, never with a deploy), `grants` (the handles, each carrying the address it was issued for), `grant_events` (append-only history whose NEWEST row is the effective state), `cred_refs` (where a secret lives and under which environment variable NAME -- never its value), `usage` (append-only consumption, which is what makes counts and rates real) and `audit` (every request, the refused ones first).
description.use_when: Inside the access hive only. `grants`, `grant_events`, `usage` and `audit` are written by ./policy, ./invoke and ./sweep; a fourth writer is a bug even where the substrate allows it. `policy` and `cred_refs` are written by NOBODY in here -- the three code cells only select from them -- which is why `contract.write_surface` is declared (GH #260: a transfer import would write policy rows in bulk past every comparison) and `params.write_surface` deliberately is NOT: enabling a rule is the operator's gesture from outside the scope, and a cell-level seal would leave a fresh broker inert forever. See the hive README, `The honest limit`.
description.not_in_scope: It holds NO secret, and it is not the cell that does: this one keeps the CATALOGUE (`cred_refs` is a table of NAMES), and a credential VALUE lives in `./vault` -- sealed at rest in the vault's own `cell.db`, and leaving it only as a SEALED BOX on `deliver`, addressed to an ephemeral key the requester minted for that one call -- never in the clear and never back to whoever asked. An encrypted table HERE would be a second one, with a key that would come from the same .env it claims to improve on. No row-level visibility either -- whoever holds an edge into this cell reads unfiltered, which is why the port discipline is the guarantee.
